title: Big O Flashcard Feed
summary: Passive flashcards for Big O notation, program-flow recognition, production tradeoffs, snippets, and interview explanations.
audience: Engineers studying algorithmic complexity for practical code review and interview fluency.

cards.title: Growth Shape
cards.prompt: Big O describes how work grows as input grows, not exact runtime in milliseconds.
cards.explanation: Use Big O to reason about code shape and scaling risk before specific hardware, constants, or benchmarks dominate the conversation.

cards.title: Dominant Term Review
cards.prompt: A function that does n^2 pair checks and then a linear pass is still O(n^2).
cards.explanation: The quadratic work dominates as input grows. Keep constants and smaller terms in mind for engineering, but simplify the growth label to the dominant term.

cards.title: Set Lookup Snippet
cards.prompt: Read the snippet as a reminder that setup work can reduce repeated query work.
cards.explanation: Building the set is O(n), but each later membership check is usually O(1) average case.
cards.code:
const allowed = new Set(allowedSkus);
items.filter((item) => allowed.has(item.sku));

cards.title: Two Sum Tradeoff
cards.prompt: Explain the time and space tradeoff between brute force Two Sum and the hash-map solution.
cards.explanation: Brute force checks pairs in O(n^2) time with O(1) extra space. The hash-map solution uses O(n) space to reduce time to O(n).

cards.title: Halving Work
cards.prompt: Binary search is O(log n) because each comparison can discard about half the remaining search space.
cards.explanation: The sorted-data precondition is the important detail. Without sorted or indexed data, the program cannot safely discard half.

cards.title: Request Path Budget
cards.prompt: The same O(n log n) sort can be fine in a nightly job and wrong in a user-facing request path.
cards.explanation: Complexity review must include where the work runs, how often it repeats, and which user or system budget owns the latency.

cards.title: Graph Dimensions
cards.prompt: Why do graph problems often describe complexity as O(V + E)?
cards.explanation: Nodes and edges can grow independently. A traversal may visit each vertex and each edge, so both dimensions belong in the explanation.

cards.title: Nested Loop Snippet
cards.prompt: Read the snippet as a reminder that nested loops can multiply independent input sizes.
cards.explanation: If users and permissions can grow independently, the work is O(users * permissions), not just a vague O(n).
